paras: The threatened lynching of William Washington followed the killing of Mrs. Mary Miller, the young wife of farmer John Miller, near Ellinger, Texas, in late December 1887, for which Washington, a Black former servant of the family, was arrested. Wire dispatches of December 31 and January 1 predicted that he would be lynched within hours, and one reported proposals that he be tortured to death. No lynching was reported; in October 1888 papers reported that a William Washington, convicted of the rape and murder of a white woman near Columbus, Texas, was hanged there before a crowd of 2,000 to 3,000.

According to a Galveston dispatch of December 30, John Miller, described as a wealthy farmer, attended a wedding at a neighbor's house on a Wednesday night and on returning the next morning found his young wife dead in a field near the house with her throat cut. Washington, identified only as "a negro," was suspected and could not at first be found. A one-sentence summary carried in Midwestern weeklies said Mrs. Miller had been "taken from bed by a negro, carried to a field near the house, assaulted and murdered."

A special from Ellinger, relayed from Galveston on December 31, said Washington had been captured "last night" and had confessed. A Columbus special to the St. Paul Daily Globe, dated January 1, gave a fuller version in which Sheriff Townsend and his deputies seized the "colored boy" at New Ulm, in an adjoining county, and brought him to Ellinger "under a heavy guard." In the confession the sheriff attributed to him, Washington said he entered the room as Mrs. Miller put out the light, chased her into a field when she broke loose, cut her throat and assaulted her.

Both treated a lynching as imminent: the Savannah Morning News printed the line "It is expected that he will be lynched to-night," while the Globe's correspondent wrote that Washington "will be lynched before many hours." The same correspondent added that some proposed he be "slowly tortured to death" and that local feeling held hanging or shooting to be "an inadequate penalty."

Ten months later, a Columbus dispatch of October 22 reported that William Washington, "colored," had been hanged near the town the previous Saturday in the presence of 2,000 people. He had been "charged and convicted of outraging and murdering a white woman near here," the dispatch said, had confessed, and had professed religion and joined a church a few days before. The October items named neither the victim nor Ellinger, so their identification with the January case rests on the shared name, the Columbus dateline, the charge and the confession. No account of the trial itself was found.

All the coverage came from white papers, beginning with specials to the Galveston News that were relayed by wire. Headlines treated Washington's guilt as settled: the Savannah Morning News ran "LYNCHING LOOKED FOR. A Black Flend Murders a Woman and Then Outrages Her," and the St. Paul Daily Globe headed its account "A MOB'S OPPORTUNITY." Neither paper questioned the expected lynching.

The Butte Semi-Weekly Miner printed the first, pre-arrest dispatch under the heading "The Sight that Met His Gaze," and weeklies in Minnesota and Dakota ran the one-sentence summary in their news columns on January 5 and 6. The October hanging traveled as a short wire item from Pennsylvania to Dakota, under headlines such as "Two Thousand People Saw Him Hang" and "A Public Execution in Texas."

The two Galveston specials differ on timing: the earlier one placed Miller at a neighbor's wedding on Wednesday night, with the body found the next morning, while the later one dated the killing to "Thursday night last." Accounts of the attack also differ, since the confession reported by the Globe has Mrs. Miller fleeing from the bedroom into a field, while the wire summary says she was taken from bed and carried there. Figures for the crowd at the October hanging ranged from 2,000 in the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer to 3,000 in the Maysville Evening Bulletin and other papers.
